query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Optimized friction stir processing with in situ injection of a tailored high-entropy alloy filler powder will produce a refined, graded, and crack-free repair zone that exhibits mechanical performance on par with or superior to traditional fusion welding methods, even under aggressive thermal cycling up to 900°C.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-value component made from a high-entropy or crack‐sensitive alloy that has sustained damage making fusion-welding repair ineffective due to hot cracking.
generation.intervention: Apply a friction stir processing approach using a non-consumable tool operating at 300–600 rpm below 0.5Tm with integrated, optimized in situ injection of a CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy filler powder.
generation.conditions: Processing is performed in the solid state (temperature maintained below 0.5Tm) with controlled traverse speeds and optimized tool and filler injection design, followed by post-process thermal cycling tests up to 900°C.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement induced by friction stir processing combined with a graded transition zone formed by the homogeneous dispersion of the injected filler powder.
generation.mechanism: The friction stir process induces severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization that eliminates preexisting micro-cracks. Simultaneously, the in situ injected high-entropy filler, when uniformly integrated, creates a seamless compositional gradient between the repair overlay and the parent material, minimizing thermal expansion mismatches and the associated tensile stresses that cause hot cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized repair will yield a fine, homogeneous, crack‐free microstructure with mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility, and creep resistance) comparable or superior to traditional fusion-welded repairs, particularly under high-temperature and aggressive thermal cycling conditions.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion welding results in hot cracking due to high-temperature gradients, compositional discontinuities, and unfavorable thermal expansion mismatches.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective as long as processing temperatures remain below ~0.5Tm, the filler powder is uniformly dispersed, and service conditions do not exceed thermal cycling up to 900°C.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty over achieving perfect homogeneous integration of the filler powder. Process scale-up and optimization of tool design are critical to prevent compositional inhomogeneity and ensure reliable mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Process small-scale samples of the damaged component using the optimized friction stir processing with filler injection. Conduct comparative studies with samples repaired using traditional fusion welding under identical conditions, including post-process thermal cycling up to 900°C.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via SEM and EBSD to assess grain size and the presence of cracks.
Chemical and compositional uniformity mapping to verify homogeneous filler integration.
Mechanical testing (tensile tests, ductility measurements) of the repaired zones.
Thermal cycling tests to evaluate repair stability under aggressive conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the repaired zone exhibits significant compositional inhomogeneity, the presence of cracks, or mechanical properties that are inferior to or significantly different from those of the traditional fusion welding repair under identical conditions, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

Fig. 6 illustrates the experimental thermal expansion coefficient of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. According to the figure, the thermal expansion coefficient of the alloy at 900–1100 K varies between 23 × 10−6 and 25 × 10−6, which is higher than that of austenitic stainless steel (16 × 10−6–17 × 10−6 K−1) in the same temperature range. Hence, the welded joints of the alloy will result in greater tensile stresses during solidification, and they are more susceptible to thermal cracking. Meanwhile, compared to the stainless steel plate, the aluminum alloy base plate has higher thermal conductivity. This indicates that the heat dissipation is more rapid and the weld cooling rate is faster, leading to a larger tensile strain rate. proposals.material_system: High-value component made from a high-entropy alloy (or similar crack‐sensitive alloy) that is prone to hot cracking under fusion welding conditions
proposals.intervention: Solid-state repair using friction stir processing (FSP) combined with in situ injection of a tailored high-entropy alloy filler powder (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-based formulation)
proposals.conditions: Process the damaged zone using a friction stir tool at tool rotation speeds of 300–600 rpm and traverse speeds tuned to keep the peak temperature below the fusion point (approximately 0.5Tm), with local filler powder injection. Follow with post-process thermal cycling tests up to 900°C to mimic aggressive operating conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement in the repaired zone; formation of a refined, crack-free microstructure that transitions seamlessly from the parent metal to the repair overlay
proposals.mechanism: The friction stir tool mechanically stirs and plastically deforms the surface layers, inducing dynamic recrystallization that eliminates preexisting micro-cracks and homogenizes the microstructure. The locally injected high-entropy filler powder further mixes with the workpiece, forming a graded transition that minimizes compositional discontinuities and thermal expansion mismatches that typically trigger hot cracking during fusion processes.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The repaired region will exhibit a fine, homogenized, and crack‐free microstructure with enhanced ductility and comparable or improved mechanical performance (e.g., tensile and creep resistance) relative to the damaged baseline. In contrast to traditional fusion welding repairs, the intervention will avoid the formation of hot cracks, ensuring reliable performance under thermal cycling and aggressive service conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By avoiding melting altogether, friction stir processing mitigates the high-temperature gradients and liquid-phase related stresses that lead to hot cracking. Coupling FSP with a tailored filler allows in situ formation of a compatible, graded microstructure that bridges compositional differences. This approach provides an effective repair option for high-value components that cannot be reliably rejoined by fusion welding, thus extending service life without full replacement.

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposed intervention directly tackles the hot-cracking issue by completely avoiding melting, which is the root cause of cracking in traditional fusion welding, thereby enabling repair of high-value components made from crack‐sensitive alloys.
critiques.constraints: The intervention respects the constraints by operating in the solid-state regime (below 0.5Tm) and by using a tailored high-entropy alloy filler that aims to match the chemistry and thermal properties of the parent material, thus avoiding large thermal expansion mismatches or deleterious microstructural transformations.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound. Friction stir processing is well-known to induce dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement, and the concept of in situ filler powder injection to form a compositional gradient that minimizes discontinuities is plausible, especially for high-entropy alloys. However, the specifics of in situ powder integration require careful process control.
critiques.feasibility: FSP is an established and feasible method in materials processing, as evidenced by previous work (e.g., PMC6742669 and PMC10730726). The addition of filler injection is more novel but can be built upon existing techniques in surface composite fabrication.
critiques.evidence: Multiple records support the use of solid-state processes like FSP for microstructural refinement in HEAs and for avoiding the melting-related defects seen in welding (e.g., PMC11382193 shows hot-cracking in fusion processes, while PMC6742669 and PMC10730726 demonstrate that FSP can yield refined, crack-free microstructures).
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in achieving uniform mixing of the injected high-entropy filler powder with the workpiece material. Inadequate integration could result in compositional inhomogeneity, potential weak zones, or failure to fully mitigate hot-cracking risk.
critiques.fix: Optimize the design of the FSP tool and the filler injection system to ensure homogeneous dispersion and integration of the filler powder during processing.

decision.rationale: The proposed friction stir repair with in situ high-entropy filler injection directly addresses hot-cracking by avoiding full melting, and the critic’s concern regarding uniform powder integration is manageable with an optimized tool and injection system. This approach provides a coherent solution to repair high-value crack‐sensitive components under aggressive operating conditions.
